metadata.name: Ecodesign for Go
metadata.description: Ecodesign rules for Go code: bounded goroutines, released resources, streamed bodies, reused clients, no polling.

concurrence.name: Go — concurrency
concurrence.description: Every goroutine needs a way to end, every pool a bound (RGESN Algorithms, GR491_Backend_4).

rules.title: Goroutine with no way to stop
rules.description: A goroutine started inside a loop or a handler, with no cancellation and no bound, keeps running after the work that needed it is gone. It holds its stack, its closures and whatever it is blocked on, and a leak that grows with traffic ends as an out-of-memory restart.
rules.recommendation: Give every goroutine a termination path: a context you propagate, a bounded worker pool, or an errgroup you wait on. Bound the queue that feeds it as well.

example.good:
g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)
g.Go(func() error { return work(ctx) })

rules.note: Starting a goroutine is normal Go; the pattern flags the place to check that this one can end. A file that already propagates a context, waits on a WaitGroup or uses errgroup stays silent.

rules.title: Blocking sleep used as a scheduler
rules.description: A loop that sleeps and polls burns CPU and network on a schedule of its own, whether or not anything changed, and keeps the machine out of low-power states.
rules.recommendation: Drive the work from an event: a channel, a ticker you can stop, a webhook, a queue. Where polling is unavoidable, widen the interval and document the stop condition.
rules.note: time.Sleep is legitimate for backoff between retries. A file that already uses a ticker, a select or a timeout context stays silent.

ressources.name: Go — resources and I/O
ressources.description: Release what you open, stream what is large, reuse what is costly to build (RGESN Backend/Hosting).

rules.title: Response body never closed
rules.description: An HTTP response body that is not closed holds the connection out of the pool. The pool then opens another one, repeats the TLS handshake, and the file descriptors accumulate until the process runs out.
rules.recommendation: defer resp.Body.Close() right after checking the error, on every path including the ones that return early.
rules.note: The rule goes quiet as soon as the file closes a body anywhere. Where a file makes several calls, check that each one closes its own.

rules.title: Whole body read into memory
rules.description: io.ReadAll on a response or a file allocates memory proportional to the payload. On a large or attacker-controlled body that is a memory spike the process pays for, where a stream would have used a fixed buffer.
rules.recommendation: Decode straight from the reader (json.NewDecoder(resp.Body)), copy with io.Copy, or bound the read with io.LimitReader.

rules.title: HTTP client built per call
rules.description: A client created for each request loses the connection pool it was carrying: every call redoes DNS resolution and the TLS handshake, for latency and CPU that a shared client pays once.
rules.recommendation: Build one client at package or service level, with timeouts and transport limits, and share it. It is safe for concurrent use.
rules.note: A single client built once at package level is exactly the recommendation, so a file that declares it as a var stays silent.

rules.title: Outbound request with no deadline
rules.description: A request with no context and no timeout can hold a goroutine, a connection and whatever memory it references for as long as the remote end stays silent. Under load those pile up faster than they clear.
rules.recommendation: Use http.NewRequestWithContext with a context.WithTimeout, and set the client's own Timeout as a backstop.
rules.note: The rule goes quiet as soon as the file builds one request with a context, or sets a client timeout anywhere. Where a file issues several requests, check that each one carries a deadline.
